{
    "id": "07-tool-use/api-pagination",
    "title": "API Pagination",
    "category": "07-tool-use",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Walk paged API result sets to completion — cursor or page parameters, per-request limits, and a terminal condition — without missing or double-processing records.",
    "body": "API Pagination Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A paged response is a promise that the full list exists and a refusal to hand it over at once. This skill treats the pager as an explicit state machine: the request carries the continuation token, the response carries the next one, and iteration stops only when the API says it is finished. Rate limits are part of the traversal, not an error condition — a pager that ignores them will be right about the data and wrong about the budget. When to Use Use whenever an API returns lists with a cursor, page token, or offset parameter — directories, event logs, resource listings — and the task needs the complete set. Do not fetch all pages when the task only needs a bounded prefix; a search that stops at the first match should not traverse the whole corpus. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The paged API operation to traverse | | | | Yes | Records requested per page, within the API maximum | | | | Yes | What to do with each record as pages arrive | | | | No | The request budget the traversal must respect | Procedure 1. Read the API contract for its pagination style — cursor, offset, or page token — before writing any loop. 2. Issue the first request with the largest page size the API allows, because fewer round trips is fewer chances to rate-limit. 3. Hand each record to the collector as its page arrives, rather than accumulating every page in memory. 4. Persist the continuati on token between requests, and treat an absent or null token as the terminal condition — never a missing key. 5. Respect the rate limit: back off when the API says so, and prefer the retry-after guidance over a fixed sleep when it is offered. 6. Record the traversal outcome — pages fetched, records seen, terminal reason — so an incomplete walk is detectable after the fact. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Each record delivered as its page arrives | | | | Page count, record count, and terminal condition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Dropped records | A null next-token value misread as an error | Treat the documented null token as the sole terminal condition | | Double processing | A retried page appended twice | Make the collector idempotent or track the last token processed | | Memory blowout | Every page held until the end | Collect per page; never retain the full traversal | | Rate-limit storms | Consecutive throttled responses during the walk | Back off on the first signal, not the third | | Silent truncation | A walk stopped early and nobody noticed | Report pages, records, and stop reason at t he end | Security and Authority Boundary Continuation tokens are credentials for data position: they can leak record ranges and query context when logged or shared, so treat them as sensitive in logs, and scope every traversal to the caller whose credentials opened it — a walk must never resume under a different principal. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Stripe API documentation on pagination (https://docs.stripe.com/api/pagination). 2. Wikipedia's overview of rate limiting (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_limiting). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "id": "07-tool-use/api-version-pinning",
    "title": "API Version Pinning",

    "description": "Pin every external API to a specific, recorded version — and upgrade as a deliberate, tested change — so upstream evolution never rewrites behavior silently.",
    "body": "API Version Pinning Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An unpinned API call is a bet on someone else's release calendar. This skill removes the bet: each external dependency is pinned to a concrete version in configuration, the pin is visible in code review, and upgrades happen as deliberate changes with a diff, a changelog read, and a test pass. Pinning goes further than a version number where the provider allows it — dated pins and versioned endpoints record the wire behavior the tests actually exercised. When to Use Use for every external API integration that reaches production, and pin in configuration rather than in a dependency default. Do not pin so hard that upgrades never happen; an integration left on an unsupported version is a slower, quieter failure mode. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The external API or SDK being integrated | | | | Yes | The concrete version recorded in configuration | | | | Yes | How and when deliberate upgrades are scheduled | Procedure 1. Record the pin in configuration, not in a lockfile default or a floating latest, so it appears in review and in audits. 2. Read the provider versioning model — dated pins, endpoint versions, deprecation windows — and record the model beside the pin. 3. Subscribe to change: watch the changelog or deprecation feed for the pinned version, and treat deprecation notices as scheduled work. 4. Upgrade deliberately: new pin, changelog diff read, integration tests r un, and the change shipped as its own reviewable commit. 5. Roll back the pin, not the code, when an upgrade misbehaves — the pin is the smallest reversible unit. 6. Audit pins periodically: a pin on an unsupported version is a defect even while everything still works. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Dependency to recorded version, with pinning model | | | | Deliberate upgrades with date, diff, and test evidence | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating latest | The SDK default changes behavior on its own | Pin every integration in reviewed configuration | | Missed deprecation | A deprecation window closed unwatched | Watch the changelog feed for the pinned version | | Surprise upgrades | A dependency bump upgraded the wire behavior | Upgrade the pin in its own reviewed change | | Unauditable pins | Nobody can list what versions run in production | Keep pins in config and audit them periodically | | Unreviewable rollback | A bad upgrade reverted by editing code | Move the pin back, the smallest reversible unit | Security and Authority Boundary Version pins interact with trust: upgrading an API client changes what is sent and to whom, so pin changes deserve security review like any dependency change, and a pin must never be loosened to make an unrelated integration problem go away. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Stripe documentation on API versioning and upgrades (https://docs.stripe.com/ upgrades). 2. The twelve-factor app guidance on configuration (https://12factor.net/config). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "body": "Streaming Tool Output Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some tool calls are streams pretending to be calls: search results that arrive page by page, logs that emit lines for minutes, models that produce tokens before the sentence is done. This skill treats the output as a sequence with a protocol — a delimiter or an event frame — and consumes it incrementally: parse what has arrived, hold a bounded remainder for the incomplete tail, and surface progress to whoever is waiting. The alternative is buffering everything, which turns a long result into a long silence followed by a large object. When to Use Use for long-running or high-volume tool output — event streams, incremental search, anything that delivers value before completion. Do not add streaming machinery to short, fast calls; a buffered read of a small response is simpler and equally correct. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The tool output arriving incrementally | | | | Yes | The boundary that separates records, newline by default | | | | Yes | What to run on each complete record as it parses | | | | No | Maximum bytes held for an incomplete tail | Procedure 1. Fix the protocol first: know what delimits a record — a newline, a frame header, a terminator — before reading a byte. 2. Read incrementally and split on the delimiter, keeping the incomplete tail in a buffer rather than discarding it. 3. Dispatch each complete record to the handler immediately, so downstream work overlaps with the remaining stream. 4. Bound the buffer: a tail that grows past its limit is a protocol violation, and streaming must fail loudly, not allocate quietly. 5. Surface progress — records seen, bytes read — so a slow stream is observable while it runs. 6. Handle terminal conditions distinctly: end-of-stream, error frame, and cancellation are different events and must close differently.     "body": "Tool Output Validation Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tool result is untrusted input with a confident tone: it arrives as a string, a dict, or a truncated fragment, and whatever shape it claims is a claim. This skill moves the checking to the boundary: each expected output is declared as a schema, each result is validated on arrival, and a failure is reported as a structured error with the offending path — not smuggled into the conversation for the caller to misread. Validation failures are normal control flow, not exceptions to silence. When to Use Use whenever a tool result feeds decisions — structured data, numeric values, identifiers — and especially when results come from external services outside your control. Do not validate ad hoc fields nobody consumes; a schema that checks everything protects nothing in particular and costs every call. Validate on arrival: check presence first, then types, then value constraints such as ranges or enum membership. 3. Collect every violation with its path rather than failing on the first, so one pass describes the whole gap. 4. Route failures by policy: reject the result, attempt a bounded repair, or re-request once with a corrected call. 5.     "description": "Reuse identical tool calls that already succeeded — keyed by operation and arguments — so repeat work costs a lookup instead of another remote round trip.",
    "body": "Tool Result Caching Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every tool call that returns the same answer for the same arguments is a cache wearing a network costume. This skill makes that explicit: a deterministic operation gets a cache key built from its identity and its arguments, responses are stored with a time-to-live and a staleness policy, and a hit must be marked as cached so downstream consumers know what they are reading. The discipline is deciding which calls are cacheable — deterministic and side-effect-free — before caching anything. When to Use Use for deterministic, read-only calls whose arguments repeat across a session or pipeline — enrichment lookups, reference data fetches, idempotent reads. Do not cache calls whose results depend on hidden state, side effects, wall-clock time, or caller identity, and do not let a cache silently answer after the underlying data contract changes underneath it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The tool operation being cached | | | | Yes | The call arguments that form part of the cache key | | | | Yes | How long a cached response may be served | | | | No | What happens on expiry — refetch, or serve-stale-while-refreshing | Procedure 1. Confirm the operation is deterministic and side-effect-free; anything with hidden state is disqualified before a key is built. 2. Build the cache key from the operation identity and the full, normalized argument set, so two calls that differ only in formatting still share an entry. 3. Store the response with its time-to-live and the timestamp of the fetch, not the timestamp of the read. 4. On a hit, return the cached value marked as cached, with its original fetch time, so consumers can reason about staleness. 5. On expiry, refetch — or serve stale while refreshing when the policy allows — and record the miss rate per operation. 6. Invalidate by key when the underlying data is known to change, and treat a change in the data contract as a full invalidation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The deterministic key for the operation and arguments | | | | The stored response with fetch timestamp and provenance | | | | Hit rate, miss rate, and staleness served per operation | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Stale answers | The underlying source changed within the TTL | Keep TTLs short for volatile data and invalidate on known writes | | Key collisions | Different calls normalized into one key | Include th e full argument set and operation in the key | | Side-effect caching | A non-deterministic call got cached | Cache only deterministic, read-only operations | | Silent provenance | Consumers cannot tell a hit from a fetch | Mark every served value as cached with its fetch time | | Unbounded growth | Entries accumulate without eviction | Bound the cache and evict on a replacement policy | Security and Authority Boundary A cache is a copy of data outside its origin's access control: cache stores inherit the sensitivity of what they hold, so entries holding user-scoped or restricted data must be keyed to the caller's scope and evicted on scope change, never shared across principals. Give every parameter a type, a description, and where possible a bound; unbounded parameters are rejections in waiting. 3. Prefer closed enums over free text wherever the value space is known. 4.
